en: Sometimes many people lose in the same way because the harm has a single source. These are not separate harms that happen to look alike. It is one harm that springs from the very design of the service, and that is why it has a unity that justifies dealing with it collectively rather than person by person.

In platform environments, the harmful source may lie in the very design of the supply regime, so that the unity of the problem does not stem primarily from the empirical repetition of episodes<1>p. 774</1>
It refers to an injury produced by the very design of the supply regime, and therefore endowed with sufficient functional unity to justify collective institutional treatment.<1>p. 774</1>
<1>Law</1>Consumer by equivalence

And what about someone who bought nothing but depends on the same environment? One example is the small seller who can only sell through a large platform's store. This seller is not a consumer in the ordinary sense, yet is exposed, from a fragile position, to the platform's commercial practices, supply methods and governance.

The law allows this person to be protected as if they were a consumer. But not every participant qualifies for this protection. Only someone who is genuinely exposed, in a situation of vulnerability that matters to the law.

Once Article 29 of the CDC<1><2>1</2></1> is accepted as applicable to qualify legal entities in a factual position of vulnerability, the regime proves fully pertinent when the immaterial object in question is the enjoyment bundle in a sustained position, exploited by the holder as a product in the B2B market and offered, through the marketplace platform, to the seller (vendedor)<3>p. 434</3>

[...] although it does not fit comfortably into the traditional figure of the final purchaser as imagined in simple, linear relationships, it is exposed to the commercial practices, supply methods and private governance mechanisms of the environment in a condition of legally relevant vulnerability<1>p. 779</1>
Not every participant in a platform ecosystem will be a consumer by equivalence.<1>p. 780</1>
<1>Law</1>Competition

The same design that holds you in can keep competitors out. When the way your experience is built also gives the company an edge over others in the market, the problem is no longer only the consumer's. It also becomes a competition problem, affecting whoever could offer an alternative.

Seen this way, the IOC regime does not replace competition law. It provides an entry grammar for understanding when the architecture of the consumer's experience has already become, at the same time, the architecture of competitive advantage.<1>p. 771</1>

None of this becomes an automatic formula. The path only puts the questions in order. What form of platform governance is at stake? What duty was breached? What minimum proof can be required? How does the case qualify in law? And what response makes sense for it?
The rest is judgment, case by case, by whoever decides. What these names do is make sure the right questions get asked.

It sets out, in language that can be consulted, the path from governance structure to breached duty, minimum evidentiary requirement, legal qualification and possible institutional consequence.<1>p. 748</1>
<1>The evidence held by the platform has to come out</1><2>The evidence held by the platform has to come out</2>
When does the platform hold all the proof?

When almost everything that shows what happened stays with the platform. The system logs, your account history, the old versions of the screens and the reasons behind each decision are on its side, not yours.
What must the platform do with the records?
Keep and show the minimum records needed to reconstruct what happened. Being open to verification is part of supplying legitimately.
What can you show and what does the platform hold?

On your side, give a plausible account of what you went through, show how it fits into the game and gather what was within your reach. On the platform's side, present the records, histories, versions and technical justifications that matter for the case.
The more what happened depends on what only the platform records, the less reasonable it is to demand from you detailed proof of something that was never in your hands.
How should proof be shared according to access to the records?

The burden of proof should be shared according to who has access to it. Depending on the case, there may also be presumptions in your favor, which make certain facts count as true until proven otherwise, and a heightened duty for the platform to cooperate with the proof.
Does this mean you no longer have to explain what happened?

You still have to tell a coherent, believable story and be clear about what you are asking for. What falls away is the fiction that you and the platform are on equal footing when it comes to proof. Your lack of access to the records cannot become a wall against you.

Whenever the platform holds the elements essential to narrating, demonstrating and reconstructing the conflict, the rules of evidence must recognize that verifiability is part of the very legitimate regime of supply.<1>p. 747</1>
The corresponding duty is to preserve and disclose the minimum records needed to reconstruct the disputed event.<1>p. 747</1>

The minimum required proof, from the consumer's side, consists of a plausible account of the harmful experience, of how it fits into the ecosystem and of the accessible contextual elements<1>p. 747</1>
from the supplier's side, it requires disclosure of trails, logs, histories, versions and technically delimited justifications<1>p. 747</1>
The possible legal qualification involves dynamic redistribution of the burden of proof, presumptions in the consumer's favor and a reinforced duty of cooperation<1>p. 747</1>

This does not remove the need for plausibility, for a coherent line of argument or for a clear delimitation of what is in dispute. What it removes is the fiction of symmetry in environments whose very structure runs on asymmetry of meaning and of proof.<1>p. 736</1>
The institutional consequence is to prevent technical opacity from becoming a procedural shield<1>p. 747</1>
<1>The answer should restore what you lost</1><2>The answer should restore what you lost</2>
When does the loss call for more than money?

When the problem affects your access, the continuity of what you use or the equivalence of what you bought. Or when it affects your history, your standing among other players or what the item meant to you.
What response must the platform give?
A response that fits the kind of loss. If what you lost was a function, the response should target that function, not just a sum of money at the end.
How do you link the loss to what the platform did?

The link between the platform's decision or mechanism and the loss you suffered. And the fact that it is technically or institutionally possible to restore, undo, replace with something equivalent or correct the procedure.
What solution can restore what was lost?

The priority is to recover what was lost, when that is feasible. The solution has to match the loss you showed and what can realistically be restored. That may mean restoring access, undoing a penalty, preserving your history, replacing the item with something that serves the same function, adjusting the rules and stopping the problem from continuing. When the harm reveals a recurring pattern, you can also ask for the structure that produces it to be corrected.
What about financial compensation?

Money stays on the table. Compensation remains possible, including for harms that are not only material, when restoring is not feasible or not enough. What is rejected is treating it as the automatic answer to everything, as if every loss of this kind turned into a number without anyone looking at what was lost.

Whenever the injury affects access, continuity, equivalence, history, relational position or significant density of enjoyment, the legal response must prioritize functional restoration, reserving pecuniary compensation for cases where restoration is unfeasible or insufficient.<1>p. 748</1>
The corresponding duty is to shape protection according to the nature of the loss, aiming at the affected enjoyment and not only at its residual translation into money.<1>p. 748</1>

The minimum required proof involves demonstrating the link between the governance mechanism and the functional loss, as well as the technical or institutional possibility of restoration, reversal, equivalent substitution or procedural correction.<1>p. 748</1>

The possible legal qualification varies with the main ground at play in the case, but the institutional consequence must favor restoration of access, reversal of sanctions, preservation of history, equivalent functional substitution, governance adjustments, injunctive relief and structural correction when the harm reveals a repeatable pattern<1>p. 748</1>

In these cases, monetary compensation continues to play an important role, whether to reimburse material losses or to recognize non-pecuniary damages when present. What is rejected is turning it into the automatic, preferred response in every case, as if the injury to the IOC could always be adequately translated into a figure without regard for the structure of the enjoyment compromised.<1>p. 742</1>

Does this only happen in games?
A video game controller, a chat bubble, a shopping cart, a delivery bag and a smiling interface face, all tied by strings that run down to the same structure hidden in the floor.

Maybe you do not even play. The same goes for the artificial intelligence assistant you use for study or work and for the online store where you shop. It goes for the app that assigns rides and deliveries and for the friendly customer service that makes your complaint seem overblown.

The game was the starting point because everything is clearer there. The account, the currency, the penalties and the changes are in plain view for any player. Outside the game, the same effects usually come packaged as something inevitable, which makes them harder to see.

The movement of consolidation and transition to the procedure of dogmatic reconstruction shows with special clarity how the interactive entertainment industry, because of the continuous provision that characterizes it, operates as a conspicuous surface on which the Lex Plataformae is exposed<1>p. 497</1>
The difference is that, outside the game, the same effects tend to be presented as inevitable rather than as architectural choices<1>p. 23</1>
These traits appear with particular clarity in three digital business models: games operated as a service, marketplaces and artificial intelligence services provided through platforms.<1>p. 486</1>

The focus on electronic game platforms serves a methodological reason, not a thematic preference. These ecosystems tend to concentrate, in high resolution, the defining elements of the IOC regime<1>p. 484</1>

What these cases share is not the sector of the economy or the type of technology. It is the way the platform governs use, manages what you expect, controls what you can understand and makes it easier or harder to contest.

That is why it is not enough to look at the service's name, whether it calls itself an app, a store, a network or an assistant. What matters is the main mechanism that organizes, adjusts and remakes your experience, and makes it contestable or not. It is this mechanism, and not the sector label, that lets you compare cases that look so different at first sight.

The common ground lies not on the surface of the environment, but in the way enjoyment is governed, expectation is managed, intelligibility is modulated and contestation is made more or less practicable by private design.<1>p. 787</1>

The unit of examination lies not in the economic sector or in the marketing label of the service, but in the predominant mechanism by which the user's experience is organized, modulated, reconfigured or made contestable.<1>p. 755</1>
<1>And what if the assistant you use starts behaving differently?</1>

An artificial intelligence assistant does more than hand out stray answers. It shapes how you understand a problem, what you trust and how you decide. You bring what it says into your work, review it, correct it and ask again.

That is why the problem is not just a wrong answer here and there. What matters is the trust that keeps you using it and the chance to reconstruct what happened. If the quality of the service changes, the question is the same as with the skin. What was promised, what changed and with what effect on those who relied on it?
What is offered is an environment of cognitive orientation.<1>p. 757</1>

It is a functional infrastructure that organizes how the user understands the problem submitted, trusts the answer received, incorporates it into their decision-making, reviews it, corrects it or reassesses it in the face of error, fluctuation or change in performance.<1>p. 757</1>
The first is to treat the conflict as a mere discussion about an isolated factual error<1>p. 757</1>
the institutional possibility of reconstructing the link between promise, delivery, alteration and impact<1>p. 757</1>
<1>Who decides what you see in an online store?</1>

An online store usually says it only brings buyers and sellers together, like a neutral town square. In practice, it chooses what appears first, what stays hidden, who seems trustworthy, what can be compared and what takes a while to show up.

In other words, you do not see the market. You see it through the platform's filters. Rankings, reputation, featured placement and recommendations are not window dressing, because they are part of what the platform delivers and they weigh on your expectations, on the risk you perceive and on your choice.

Platforms of this nature do not merely connect. They select, rank, highlight, hide, bring closer, delay, prioritize and reorganize the way in which the reality of the environment becomes perceptible to the user.<1>p. 761</1>
In their formal language, they often appear as neutral meeting spaces between seller and buyer<1>p. 761</1>

Rankings, reputation, featuring, recommendation, prioritization and modulation of reach are not peripheral elements. They are part of the functional utility of the ecosystem and directly influence the formation of expectation, the assessment of risk and the possibility of rational choice.<1>p. 761</1>
<1>Who is in charge of work done through an app?</1>

Delivery and ride apps call drivers and couriers independent partners. But it is the app that hands out the calls, gives the ratings, decides who gets priority, sets the rules for accepting rides and applies the penalties.

For those who work this way, the app provides more than a payment per task. It provides the very environment in which the work becomes possible, and the app governs that environment. That is why it is not enough to look at what the contract says about autonomy. You have to look at who actually controls access to demand and who gets to stay in the flow of work.

The platform organizes access to demand, distribution of calls, minimum predictability of pay, permanence in the productive flow, reputational criteria, prioritization patterns, acceptance rules and sanction mechanisms.<1>p. 765</1>
What is provided, in functional terms, is a private infrastructure of economic possibility.<1>p. 765</1>
The instruments deployed by iFood, 99Food, Uber and 99 insist, with variations in language, on characterizing the partners as independent<1>p. 765</1>
This point is important because it prevents the analysis from being captured by excessively formal narratives about contractual autonomy.<1>p. 765</1>
<1>Why does complaining seem like an overreaction?</1>

And there is the tone. A friendly screen, kind replies, a caring manner and close, almost friend-like language can make the loss seem acceptable and the complaint seem like an overreaction, even before any dispute begins.

In many cases the conflict is managed before it even exists. The platform does not just look after your initial sign-up. It also looks after how much harm you will tolerate and how much energy you have left to react. Frustration is gradually absorbed as just part of how things are, and the complaint never gets made.
In many cases, it is governed before that.<1>p. 780</1>

The cordial interface, the assistive tone, the diffuse promise of care, merely performative transparency, the appearance of communicational horizontality and the calculated personalization of language materially make up the environment of enjoyment.<1>p. 781</1>

They function as a technique for governing perception, organizing the threshold from which the loss will be perceived as acceptable, the abuse will be read as a minor failure and contestation will be perceived as unnecessary, premature or disproportionate.<1>p. 781</1>
In this context, the platform does not manage only initial adhesion. It manages the user's tolerance of harm and their energy to react.<1>p. 781</1>
Does every platform have the same problem?

Showing the mechanism does not mean condemning the service. Not every platform reproduces the problem, and those that do are not all equally intense. Nor does every relationship mediated by technology fall under consumer protection.
The question is always the same, wherever you are. Can you know what was promised and what changed? And can you react?

The point here is not to gather digital examples under a single heading out of mere technological affinity, nor to suggest that every contemporary platform reproduces, with identical intensity, the same form of vulnerability, opacity or capture of enjoyment<1>p. 755</1>
Not every relationship economically mediated by technology will justify the application of the CDC.<1>p. 780</1>
This is not to say that every digital mediation automatically turns any good into an IOC.<1>p. 487</1>

Who is in charge after the purchase?
A maze seen from above, its walls made of contract pages standing upright. At the only exit, a hand holds a stamp. The text becomes a wall, and the wall becomes punishment.

When you created the account, you accepted the terms of use. It looks as if the rules of the game are all there, in that long text. But the rules that weigh on your daily life are almost never only on paper.

They are in the screen that shows one path and hides another, in the chat that gets cut off in the middle of a match and in the penalty that arrives without warning. The text promises and the system executes. And the penalty is applied by the same company that wrote the rule, designed the screen and keeps the records of what happened. That is why a conflict, when there is one, is rarely only about what a clause says. It is about who governs what you can do in there.

This normativity is not limited to the contractual clauses that govern the relationship on the formal plane, since it materializes in interface design, choice patterns, selective frictions and enforcement mechanisms<1>p. 27</1>

[...] since the implemented rule becomes the real mode of existence of the object and, consequently, the point at which the conflict stops being a dispute about clauses and becomes a dispute about the governance that defines what is possible in the ecosystem<1>p. 372</1>

[...] the Lex Plataformae designates a type of private ordering centered on a platform as the institutional core that defines rules, visibilities, sanctions and evidentiary regimes through continuous architecture and updating<1>p. 27</1>
What are the three layers of the platform's rule?
The platform's rule works in three layers, one on top of the other.

The first is the text. These are the terms of use, the conduct policies, the moderation rules and the criteria for taking part. There you find the permissions, the prohibitions and what is expected of you.

The second is the design. This is when the text becomes a screen, a button, a path, an access limit and a visibility criterion. In this layer, the rule stops being a sentence and starts deciding what is possible before any discussion. If the screen has no button, it makes no difference that the contract allows it.

The third is enforcement. These are the mechanisms that grade penalties, restrict features, lower your visibility, suspend the account and, at the extreme, kick you out. A rule only carries real weight when it passes through all three layers, because only then does it change what you can do and what happens to you.
The first is the internal normative text, formed by terms of service, conduct policies, moderation rules and declared criteria for participation<1>p. 364</1>

The second is the layer of architecture and implementation, in which such statements stop being simple declarations and become a configuration of possibilities through interface, flows, access patterns, visibility parameters and technical restrictions that delimit the range of the possible before any interpretive dispute.<1>p. 365</1>

The third is the layer of enforcement and sanctions, made up of enforcement mechanisms that grade consequences, apply restrictions, lower visibility, suspend features and, in extreme cases, exclude the user, reconfiguring their position in the environment.<1>p. 365</1>
The internal rule only gains normative density when it is converted into conditions of possibility by architecture and into consequences by enforcement.<1>p. 365</1>
<1><2>The law of the platform</2><3>Lex Plataformae</3></1>

In Latin, which is where the name was born, it is called Lex Plataformae, and plataformae means of the platform. But the law of the platform is not a contract sitting in a drawer. It is an order that runs like a program, aims at an economic result and seems natural because it is repeated so often.

It defines the rules, decides what is seen and what stays hidden, applies the penalties and even establishes how anything is proven in there. And it does not just announce the rules. It classifies, records, recommends, blocks, restricts and changes the very environment in which you try to use what you bought.

The name comes from another old expression, the law merchant, which referred to the rules that traders created among themselves, without depending on the law of any country. The difference is that here the center is not the practice of many traders. It is a single company, which controls the way in, the way you understand what happens and the conditions under which you can use what is yours.
The variation “plataformae” corresponds to the genitive singular of the first declension, signaling “of the platform”<1>p. 27</1>

The expression Lex Plataformae therefore seeks to name not a set of predisposed clauses, but a private ordering that is technically executable, economically oriented and semiotically naturalized.<1>p. 27</1>

[...] because, while the Lex Mercatoria is usually described as an ordering emerging from diffuse practices and multiple actors, the Lex Plataformae designates a type of private ordering centered on a platform as the institutional core that defines rules, visibilities, sanctions and evidentiary regimes through continuous architecture and updating.<1>p. 27</1>

It does not merely interpret behavior, but classifies, records, prioritizes, makes invisible, recommends, blocks, expels, restricts, monetizes and reconfigures the very environment in which the user tries to exercise enjoyment of the acquired object.<1>p. 27</1>

Lex Plataformae is an operative Latinization built by analogy with classical formulas for naming private orderings, especially the Lex Mercatoria, an expression used to designate an a-national body of rules and principles associated with the practice of international trade<1>p. 27</1>

it designates a private order whose center is not only mercantile circulation between actors, but control of the access infrastructure, of the intelligibility of the experience and of the concrete conditions for exercising the user's position<1>p. 28</1>

This law does one thing well, which is to look like custom. A practice that repeats many times starts to seem normal, as if everyone had agreed to it. But on a platform, repetition may be just the effect of a design that one company chose on its own and that you had no way to refuse.

That is why the fact that something has always been this way in the game does not prove that it is legitimate. Often, what looks like a market habit is already the product of a unilateral choice, which took hold because nobody had an alternative.

On the platform, the repetition of practices and solutions should not be naively read as a sufficient sign of normative legitimacy. Often, what presents itself as market habit or custom of the ecosystem is already the product of unilateral design, of structural informational asymmetry and of the naturalization of choices previously filtered by the architecture itself.<1>p. 28</1>
The critique is relevant because it prevents romanticizing, under the language of custom, what may in truth correspond to the technical stabilization of private impositions.<1>p. 28</1>
How does your behavior become a score?

In a reputation system, your behavior becomes a score. One online game created an Honor system. Players who show good sportsmanship earn benefits, and those who behave badly get fewer rewards and lose part of their right to talk in chat.

When you are penalized, with a temporary suspension or a chat cutoff, your score drops, your progress freezes and the account goes without certain rewards until you show, consistently, that you have changed. And the company says the score reflects behavior in and out of the game. None of this goes through any court. The penalty is built into the system itself and affects what you can do, earn and show.

In official documentation, Riot presents Honor as a system that rewards sporting conduct with additional benefits and penalizes inappropriate behavior with reduced rewards and limited communication privileges<1>p. 343</1>

In parallel, the company states that penalties such as temporary suspension and chat restrictions drop the Honor level, freeze progress in the system and make the account ineligible for rewards linked to the Hextech Crafting regime until there is consistent demonstration of behavioral “reform”<1>p. 343</1>
Official support describes Honor as a general reflection of behavior “in and out of game”<1>p. 355</1>

This does not mean the company sabotages players on purpose, and nobody needs to prove that. The point is simpler. The company builds the game, measures the matches, controls the chat channels and sets the criteria for penalties. But it does not show you how those criteria work to the same extent that it applies their effects to you.
That is why, in a conflict, the question is not only whether you broke a rule. It is also whether the criteria used to say you broke it, and to penalize you, are legitimate.

The point, therefore, is not to sustain, without internal proof, a maximalist thesis of deliberate sabotage, but to recognize that the company governs a competitive environment that is structurally opaque, probabilistic and administered by internal criteria whose deeper intelligibility is not shared with the consumer to the same degree that their effects are imposed on them.<1>p. 343</1>

Seen this way, the central question is no longer only whether the user broke a rule and comes to include the legitimacy of the very criteria by which the deviation is produced, read and punished.<1>p. 343</1>
<1>Power and subjectivity</1>Choice architecture
Nobody forbids you anything. The path the company wants you to take just becomes easier, more rewarded and more visible, while the other one becomes more costly, more frustrating and harder to find.

It is like a supermarket that puts the candy at eye level and the vegetables at the back of the store. You are still free to choose, but you choose along a route that someone designed. In the game, this goes beyond the options that appear on the screen, because it includes the consequences that make one path rewarded and the other painful.

Transposed to platform governance, this means that choice architecture is not limited to the presentation of options, because it also involves managing the consequences that make certain trajectories more fluid, rewarded and legible, while others become more costly, frustrating or marginal<1>p. 337</1>
Informational domination, thus, bears not only on what the consumer knows, but on the very practical economy of their possibilities of acting.<1>p. 337</1>
<1>Law</1>Informational power
This power does not need police. It creates dependence, shapes your behavior and makes certain ways of taking part seem normal. And it uses technical means that go far beyond the contract.

One detail makes all this harder to see. The simpler the screen, the better hidden the complexity that makes the decisions behind it. You see a clean button and a friendly color, and you do not see the calculations and judgments running underneath.

Cohen is drawn on to describe the platform as a form of organizing power that produces dependencies, structures conduct and naturalizes patterns of participation through technical and institutional means that are not exhausted in the contract.<1>p. 262</1>

This becomes more acute when systems display simplicity on the surface and complexity in their internal functioning, which makes it difficult to translate underlying judgments into forms suited to public understanding<1>p. 340</1>
<1>Law</1>Practical normativity

A rule does not need to come from Congress to work as a rule. What the company calls a condition of use or an internal rule can work as a real order, imposed by whoever has power over the place. It organizes access, permanence and penalties and produces effects on many people at the same time.

That is why it is not enough to say that everything comes down to freedom of contract. And the market is not a force of nature that runs on its own, because the market is the very order it establishes.

Eros Roberto Grau contributes to recognizing that normativity can operate as an effective order imposed by an organization endowed with power, making it possible to qualify as practical governance what presents itself as a “condition of use” or an “internal rule”<1>p. 263</1>

This vocabulary makes it possible to treat internal rules, implementation architecture and enforcement mechanisms as the effective law of the environment in an operational sense, since they organize access, permanence and sanctions with concrete capacity to impose patterns and produce collective effects, without neutralizing the phenomenon as a simple formal exercise of contractual autonomy<1>p. 364</1>
In this sense, the warning that “the legal order of the market prevails”, understood not as something that the market ontologically is, but as “the order that it establishes”<1>p. 378</1>
<1>Power and subjectivity</1>Psychopolitics

The rank does not order you to play more. You are the one who wants to climb. Behind the visible rank there is a secret number that measures you, and the company says the rank exists precisely to translate this number into a form you can follow. What you see is the position, and the calculation stays hidden.

So you chase a criterion you cannot see, of your own free will, and leisure turns into self-exploitation. Nobody needs to threaten you, because the fear of dropping is enough to make you invest more time and attention. And doing more is not enough. You also have to be the right kind of player, well-behaved and well-rated, to keep your access to the whole experience.
When explaining the system, official support states that MMR is secret and that rank exists as a mechanism to translate this MMR into an accessible and progressive form for the player<1>p. 354</1>
The player's freedom is organized as a voluntary search for conformity to the criterion that measures them, even when the criterion is opaque<1>p. 354</1>
For this reason, the ranked climb tends to transform leisure into a regime of rational self-exploitation.<1>p. 354</1>

Discipline, here, does not present itself as prohibition, but as a permanent summons to invest time, attention and performance so as not to lose public commensurability in the environment.<1>p. 354</1>

In League of Legends, psychopolitics manifests itself not only as an incentive to “do more”, but also as an inducement to “be the right way” if the goal is to remain eligible for the full experience of the ecosystem<1>p. 355</1>
How far does the game's rule reach into your computer?

The law of the platform can go beyond the screen and reach your computer. To protect competition against cheating, one game began to require an anti-cheat program that runs at the deepest layer of the operating system, the same layer that controls how the machine works. This program starts up with the computer, even before you open the game, and can stop you from playing if it is turned off or removed.

The terms of use also admit that the company may monitor the use of its services on your own device, and not only on its servers. The problem here goes beyond the annoyance of an invasive program. The rule no longer applies only during the match and starts to redraw how much control you have over your own equipment.
When protection of the IOC's competitive environment comes to depend on software loaded at kernel level, that is, on the deepest and most privileged layer of the operating system<1>p. 521</1>

Riot's own official communications show that Vanguard is presented as a system composed of a client and a kernel-mode driver, started at computer boot and maintained as a structural condition of enjoyment in more than one game ecosystem, with the possibility of preventing use of the service if it is disabled or removed<1>p. 521</1>
Riot contractually admits the possibility of actively monitoring the use of its services not only on its own servers, but also on the consumer's computer or device<1>p. 521</1>

This fact shifts the legal problem beyond an intuitive irritation with “intrusive” software. What is at stake is the redefinition of the material boundaries of the user's sovereignty over their own equipment.<1>p. 521</1>
<1>Consumer-citizen</1><2><3>Consumer-citizen</3></2>

So you are not just a customer. You are a consumer, because you bought something and have a legitimate expectation of using it. But your presence inside depends on rules of belonging and continuity that someone else sets, and on penalties that change your standing.

That is why you can also be called a citizen, in a very precise sense. Not a citizen of a country, with a nationality and a Constitution, but a participant in an environment governed by rules, design and penalties. When the company changes these conditions on its own, it changes, in practice, the very thing you are using.
The consumer-citizen is the subject who acquires IOCs whose utility is realized as functional permanence in an ecosystem, and not as the isolated delivery of a transferred good.<1>p. 379</1>
They are a consumer because there is acquisition and a legitimate expectation of enjoyment.<1>p. 379</1>
analytical sense that their presence in the environment depends on conditions of belonging and continuity set by private governance<1>p. 380</1>

Citizenship here does not concern nationality, sovereignty or classical constitutional status. It designates practical conditions of participation and permanence in an environment governed by internal rules, architecture and enforcement, in which the unilateral alteration of these conditions reconfigures, in practice, the very object enjoyed.<1>p. 380</1>
<1>Power and subjectivity</1>Digital citizenship

Digital citizenship, here, is not a handbook of good behavior on the internet. It is a lens for seeing what can be governed in a connected environment, such as access, communication, commerce and security, without turning every problem into the user's fault.
To delimit what is at stake without inflating the argument, the concept of digital citizenship is drawn on as a parameter, and not as a handbook.<1>p. 380</1>

Its formulation makes it possible to treat digital citizenship as an operational grid of what can be governed in the connected environment, without turning the discussion into the user's fault.<1>p. 380</1>
They are: digital access, digital commerce, digital communication<1>p. 380</1>

You are also at stake. In a game, your place depends on being seen, being recognized and belonging to a group, so losing reputation, visibility or recognition is not a mere annoyance. That loss can strike at the core of what you use even when your access continues, and the challenge is to measure it with objective criteria.
In digital ecosystems, the value offered and enjoyed is not exhausted in instrumental utilities, because it depends on regimes of visibility, recognition, belonging and reputation<1>p. 456</1>
The point that must now be addressed is how to define relevant losses that cannot be downgraded to “displeasure” or treated as a side effect.<1>p. 456</1>

The problem is to make them legally tractable through objective delimitations and criteria of controllability, including in order to capture losses that affect the enjoyment bundle even when there is no total interruption<1>p. 457</1>
<1>Law</1>Categories that keep pace with technology

This has happened before. At the end of the nineteenth century, instant photography and a growing press began to intrude on people's lives in ways the old law could not reach. That was when people argued for a right to privacy, the right to be let alone.

Adjusting the categories of law, in these cases, is not moralism or a grudge against technology. It means keeping the effects of new forms of power and intrusion under control when technology changes the scale at which people become vulnerable.

In their article, Warren and Brandeis <1>([201-?])</1> argue that recent inventions and expanding business practices intensified forms of intrusion that the legal order, if it remains tied to earlier schemes, cannot adequately capture.<2>p. 347</2>
From there, the authors argue for the recognition of a right to privacy as a legitimate right to be let alone<1>p. 347-348</1>

When the technical environment reorganizes vulnerability at scale, legal reconstruction is not moralism, but a necessary response to keep the effects of new forms of power and intrusion controllable in institutional terms.<1>p. 348</1>
So does the platform become a State?

The platform does not become a State because of this, nor does it stand above the law of the country. The law of the platform does not replace Brazilian law. It is a layer of private rules that sits between you and what you bought, and that the law cannot treat as a mere technical backdrop. Nor is it about taking any game dispute to the Constitution.

What can be demanded is proportional to the power the company exercises. Transparency that actually serves a purpose, a minimum of stability, reasons that can be checked, a real way to contest and the restoration of what was lost.

The Lex Plataformae, thus understood, does not replace State law or eliminate the application of the public legal order. It designates, rather, the private normative layer that interposes itself between the subject and enjoyment, organizing the concrete experience of consumption by means that the Law cannot treat as a mere technological backdrop.<1>p. 28</1>
This does not mean equating the platform with the State or constitutionalizing every private dispute<1>p. 348</1>
This characterization blocks the generic constitutionalization of the litigation and avoids the statist leap.<1>p. 380</1>
For this reason, proportional parameters of qualified transparency, minimum stability, verifiable reasoning, contestability and restoration are required.<1>p. 364</1>
<1>A penalty needs a reason and a chance to defend yourself</1><2>A penalty needs a reason and a chance to defend yourself</2>
When does a penalty go too far?

When your access, your permanence, your visibility or your chance to complain depend on penalties that nobody explains. Or on hurdles placed in front of only some people, on a cost too high to push back or on a way back that is much harder than the way in. It is the account blocked or banned without explanation, with an appeal route that leads nowhere. When the account is closed, access to everything in it goes too, including what you bought.
What must the platform do before penalizing?
Follow procedures that can be understood, give a reason that can be checked, let you contest in a reasonable way and not treat you arbitrarily.
How do you document the penalty and the attempt to contest it?
The records of the penalty, the appeal route that existed, the criteria used, the hurdles to undoing the measure and what it did to the continuity of your experience.
What review can be requested for the penalty?

If the penalty has no verifiable reason or no reasonable appeal route, it may be possible to have it reviewed or reversed. You can also ask the platform to fulfill its procedural duties and to create or improve a real appeal route. When the problem happens to many people, you can also ask for the penalty system as a whole to be corrected.
So the platform cannot penalize at all?
The platform has the power to penalize, but having that power is not enough. A penalty needs a reason that can be checked, consistency from one decision to the next and a clear way to challenge it.

Whenever access, permanence, visibility or contestation are conditioned by opaque sanctions, selective frictions, excessive costs of reaction or asymmetric reversal mechanisms, there will be an indication of abusive governance of the bond.<1>p. 746</1>

The corresponding supply duty is to ensure minimally intelligible procedures, verifiable reasoning, reasonable possibility of contestation and non-arbitrary treatment of the user in the administration of enjoyment.<1>p. 746</1>

The minimum required proof falls on sanction records, contestation flow, criteria deployed, structural difficulties of reversal and concrete impacts of the measure on the continuity of the experience.<1>p. 746</1>

The institutional consequence includes reversal or review of sanctions, procedural duties, creation or improvement of contestation mechanisms and, in structurally repetitive cases, correction of the ecosystem's enforcement regime.<1>p. 746</1>

For this reason, they must be controlled by denser criteria than the mere formal existence of sanctioning power. They require verifiable reasoning, decisional coherence and intelligible avenues of contestation.<1>p. 749</1>
Added to this is a reward architecture, with progression and grind systems, and a sanctioning architecture, with bans, restrictions, automated penalties and opaque policies<1>p. 211</1>

Why is this skin worth so much?
An armored figure at the center of a ring of silhouettes. The armor's glow comes not from the armor itself but from the gazes of the people around it, which cross and light the piece up.

A skin changes the character's look, effects and animations, and does so again in every match. Some people put a lot of money, many hours and a lot of attention into it. Seen from outside, it looks excessive to pay a high price for an outfit that does not exist off the screen.

Seen from inside, it makes sense, because inside the game the skin is a sign that everyone knows how to read. It says who you are, how long you have been playing and which group you belong to. Someone who buys a rare skin is not buying just a nice effect, but belonging, prestige and the chance of being recognized by others.
The form, the visual reading, the logic of transformation and the aesthetic experience happen as a performance repeated in each match.<1>p. 439</1>
A rare cosmetic item or a reconfigured character is valuable because it operates as a legible social sign, a marker of identity and a point of belonging within a proprietary grammar.<1>p. 104</1>
What is consumed, in this type of environment, is not only technical function, but belonging, prestige and recognition mediated by signs.<1>p. 105</1>

That is why your frustration, when the skin changes, is not a whim. An update can alter its appearance, its effects, the rarity everyone could see or its place in the game's economy. The skin stays in your account, with the same name, but no longer fits into the game world the way it used to. And it was this fit that gave value to all the time, money and attention you put into it.

The law can look at this in two ways. It can treat it as a personal heartache, something for people who get too attached, or it can treat it as the deterioration of something whose core is made of meaning and of relationships with others. Only the second reading makes it possible to take the loss seriously.
When the platform rewrites these signs, the nominal permanence of the object in the account may coexist with the emptying of what it meant and delivered.<1>p. 105</1>

This framing matters to the legal problem because it makes it possible to describe the injury as the degradation of an enjoyment bundle whose core is semiotic and relational, and not as mere subjective frustration.<1>p. 105</1>
<1>Anthropology of consumption</1>Value as judgment

The store price says little about the value of the skin, because the value of a thing does not live inside it. It is a judgment that people make and that exchange, real or imagined, confirms. A skin is valuable because many people desire it, compare it with others and consider it rare.

That is why the question that matters is not how much it costs, but what makes something seem desirable, comparable and rare. And here is the point, because it is the platform that decides the catalog, the rarity and the visibility rules. Whoever manages these things manages, in practice, the conditions of value itself.

The consequence is that the relevant question stops being “how much does it cost” and becomes “which frames make something appear desirable, comparable and rare”, because value is not inherent to the object, but a judgment produced by subjects and endorsed by a real or imagined exchange<1>p. 250</1>
If value is an effect of situated recognition, managing catalog, rarity and visibility rules (curation, windows, criteria) is managing the practical conditions of value itself.<1>p. 251</1>
<1>Anthropology of consumption</1>Consumption as ritual

The things we consume work like signs, some saying welcome and others saying keep out. Through them we align ourselves with some people, set ourselves apart from others and give meaning to what we experience. The skin does this inside the game, because it shows which crowd you belong to and who is left out.

Staying outside this circuit, therefore, is not just uncomfortable, because it means losing your voice and losing options. When you think about leaving a game, the cost is not only the money left behind, but also the risk of isolating yourself and weakening ties you formed inside it.
Douglas and Isherwood <1>(1996, p. xxiv)</1> describe goods as devices of alignment and of boundary.<2>p. 251</2>
Social life is organized by signs of adhesion and exclusion, and goods function as public marks that raise fences against the unwanted, consolidating solidarities<1>p. 251</1>
Staying out of reach of this system is not a subjective discomfort. It is a risk of practical silencing, reduction of voice and of future options<1>p. 251</1>

Douglas and Isherwood <1>(1996, p. 43)</1> formulate this by treating goods as ritual adjuncts and consumption as a ritual process whose function is to produce meaning in the unstable flow of events<2>p. 254</2>

[...] a vocabulary for describing the immaterial object of consumption as something whose social utility depends on social legibility and belonging within a managed ecosystem, which makes it possible to read the exit cost not only as patrimonial loss, but as a risk of isolation and weakening of bonds<1>p. 249</1>
What does a piece of music teach about the value of a skin?

In a piece of music, a single note says almost nothing, because the music lies in the relationship between the notes. Something similar happens with the things we consume. An isolated skin says little, because its meaning comes from the place it occupies beside the others, from what is common and what is rare.

That is why, when the platform tinkers with the whole, it tinkers with the meaning of each piece. Launching a new skin can change what yours said, even if nobody touched it. Whoever looks after the shop window also looks after the language that makes your item mean something.
The isolated item is semantically incomplete, since meaning emerges from the reciprocal position among goods, as happens in a grammar or in a musical harmony.<1>p. 249</1>
Goods operate as the hardware and software of an informational system in which meaning emerges from the relationships between things, and not from an essence stuck to each object<1>p. 249</1>

Regulating curation and circulation windows amounts to regulating the grammar by which value and belonging are expressed, because it alters the relationships that make the collection “say” something.<1>p. 249</1>
What is delivered is not just an item. The conditions of language that make this item exist as a socially legible difference within this ecosystem are maintained, or reordered.<1>p. 249</1>
<1>Anthropology of consumption</1>Meaning transfer

Where does the skin's meaning come from? It isn't born in the skin. It is poured into it. The trailer, the event, the shop window and the story around it link the skin to a mood, a type of person and a moment. Advertising works like a pipe through which meaning flows down into things.

And that meaning goes stale over time. Part of what a skin means expires, like food, and so renewal is not optional. There will always be a new collection, a new trailer and a new event to pour fresh meaning into things and take the shine off the old ones.
Advertising functions as a conduit through which meaning is continuously poured into goods<1>p. 256</1>
Renewal is not optional because part of the meaning is perishable.<1>p. 256</1>

In them, the form of presentation and the dramaturgy of the offer, expressed in shop windows, trailers, events and narratives of permanent updating, becomes a constitutive component of the experience consumed.<1>p. 99</1>
<1>Semiotics and language</1>Spectacle

The spectacle is not a pile of images but people relating to each other through images. In a match, your skin is seen, compared and commented on, and its value takes shape in that scene, which never stops.

This means the skin's promise does not sit still in the store, because it circulates as a social scene in which some people watch and others are watched. That permanent shop window is what keeps desire alive and keeps you wanting to stay.
Debord formulates this perspective by stating that the spectacle is not a set of images, but a social relationship between people mediated by images<1>p. 282</1>

Thus, the spectacle can be drawn on to understand platforms as environments in which the promise of the IOC circulates as a continuous social scene, that is, as a dynamic of visibility and comparison that stabilizes desire and permanence as part of value itself<1>p. 282</1>
<1>Semiotics and language</1>Gamification
Level, rank, achievements, win counter. When everything becomes a scoreboard, the experience is no longer just lived but measured all the time, so what matters becomes ranking well and keeping up.

Then staying in the game stops being just leisure and becomes a chore. Staying means remaining on the leaderboard, up to date and visible on a scale that the game itself manages. And the platform turns this control of time into urgency, with windows and opportunities that push you to decide again and again.

Practical life stops being merely lived and comes to be accompanied by indices of position, signals of performance and parameters of progress that make comparison permanent and cumulative.<1>p. 289</1>
In this regime, permanence takes the form of a task, because remaining comes to mean staying ranked, open to updating and legible within a scale that the ecosystem itself manages.<1>p. 289</1>

The gamification of everyday life, in this key, is not a playful device added to consumption, but the translation of value into scoreboards of relevance, in which what matters is to be positioned and updated in real time.<1>p. 289</1>

On this basis, it becomes possible to explain how the platform turns the governance of time and visibility into practical urgency, by organizing windows and opportunities as a recurring pressure to decide<1>p. 289</1>
Why does staying out of the game become costly?

Put all this together and a silent rule appears. If what you can lose is the right moment, status and belonging, being absent becomes costly. Disappear for a few weeks and you lose your position, miss the event and miss the skin that was only on sale in that window.

Absence stops being a pause and becomes a measurable fall. And the risk lies not only in the item, but in the meaning of what is lost and in the calendar, which turns delay into disadvantage, even when the skin is still there, technically accessible.

When the efficient risk is losing timing, status and belonging, the discipline of presence sets in as a technique for governing time. Absence stops being mere interruption and comes to produce measurable decline, progressive erasure and practical discontinuity, making permanence the rational way to avoid loss.<1>p. 254</1>

It is semiotic because it depends on the social meaning of what is lost, and temporal because it works through windows, calendars, cycles and rhythms that convert delay into objective disadvantage even when the immaterial object remains technically accessible.<1>p. 254</1>
<1>Political economy</1>Attention economy

What is scarce in this market is not skins, since a digital copy never runs out, and so, left to itself, the price would tend to fall. To charge for it, the company has to create scarcity by its own decision.

What actually runs out is your screen time. The longer you stay, the more the platform can observe how you behave, test stimuli and adjust the triggers that make you come back. It is this predictability that sustains the pass, the subscription, the can't-miss event and the offer that rotates every week.

The decisive economic point is simple and direct, since, in the market for immaterial goods, reproducibility would tend to dissolve the price, so that income depends on reintroducing scarcity by institutional decision<1>p. 234</1>

The decisive scarce resource is not the technical availability of the good, but the user's exposure time. Retention provides volume for observation, profiling, continuous testing of stimuli and calibration of triggers. It is this predictability that stabilizes extraction by subscription, pass, “can't-miss event”, offer rotation and successive tolls.<1>p. 249</1>
<1>Anthropology of consumption</1>Biography of things

Things have biographies too, and buying something does not define what it will become later. A skin is born rare, becomes common in a relaunch, leaves the catalog and comes back for an event, and each turn changes what it is worth and the status of whoever owns it. All this happens without it ever disappearing from your account.

The platform writes this biography. It retires items, changes their rarity, restricts how they can be obtained, repositions them around events and reorganizes what gets featured. Your name stays linked to the skin, but its story, which is what sustains the prestige and the promise, has been rewritten by someone else.
The fact that an object is bought or exchanged says nothing about its later status<1>p. 253</1>
For the immaterial object of consumption, this describes precisely why reworks, relaunches, trivializations and repositionings alter value and status without the item “disappearing”.<1>p. 253</1>

On platforms, this singularization takes the form of catalog retirement, change of rarity, restrictions on how items can be obtained, repositioning by event, recoding by meta and rearrangement of display criteria. The user's nominal ownership is maintained, but the cultural biography of the item is materially reordered, which is what sustains social utility, prestige and equivalence between promise and delivery.<1>p. 254</1>
How is a rarity manufactured?
Rarity can be manufactured. In one online game, the company created a new shelf above the top of the catalog, for skins it called Exalted, and presented them as hyper-exclusive, almost luxury goods.

To try for one, you do not buy the skin, but tokens that cost 400 of the game's currency and are worth one draw. The chance of getting the skin is very low, the guarantee only comes on the eightieth draw and everything is on sale for a limited time. This item-draw model, which imitates capsule machines, usually hides the real cost of the purchase behind the intermediate currency and odds that are hard to see.

What stands out is where the exclusivity comes from. It is not something the community comes to recognize over time, because it is a rule written into the system. The prestige comes from the rule that controls access, and not from the skin necessarily delivering more than the others.

A contemporary example of how signs of delivery can be artificially reordered to sustain value, commensurability and prestige is the creation of the Exalted tier and of the acquisition space called Sanctum, presented as a shelf “above” the traditional top of the catalog<1>p. 298</1>
The institutional justification frames Exalted as a set of “hyper-exclusive skins”, that is, goods explicitly described as luxury within the catalog<1>p. 299</1>
The Sanctum is described as an exclusive store in which the user buys Ancient Sparks<1>p. 299</1>

for 400 RP and uses them to draw rare content, with a specific “banner” for Exalted skins, along with time rotation and no guarantee of return <1>Riot Games</1><2>(Riot Games, 2025d)</2>.<3>p. 299</3>

The official description of the Sanctum records that Exalted skins are the only Tier S content of the corresponding banner, with an extremely low chance and a guarantee only on the eightieth draw, as well as availability for a limited time<1>p. 299</1>
A monetization model based on random draws of virtual items, inspired by capsule vending machines (gashapon).<1>p. 299</1>

From the perspective of IOCs, it represents an extraction architecture that conditions the enjoyment of desired goods on probabilistic mechanisms and successive draws, often hiding the real cost of acquisition through intermediate currencies and statistical opacity<1>p. 299</1>
The consequence is that exclusivity stops being a social inference and becomes architecture. Prestige is produced by rule, not by necessary material backing.<1>p. 299</1>
<1>Semiotics and language</1>Simulacrum

And what if the skin changes inside but still looks top of the line? This can happen, because value can be maintained by signs of delivery, such as a badge, a rarity frame or a featured place in the catalog. As long as the signs are still there, the promise seems kept and the circuit keeps turning.

The risk lies in what these signs hide. The platform can keep up the appearance of continuity while changing effects, restrictions, forms of access and performance. With the facade unchanged, it becomes very hard to prove that anything was lost. So the problem is not that the skin has symbolic value, but that appearance serves to erase the proof that the promise is no longer being kept.

[...] in the consumer society, the socially valued promise tends to require measurement and proof through objects and signs [...] With this, it becomes possible to sustain, without reducing the argument to a denunciation of illusion, that value can be maintained by signs of delivery and by visible criteria of equivalence, which authorizes treating the simulacrum as a mechanism capable of preserving the economic circuit of the IOC even when the relevant enjoyment changes<1>p. 296</1>

When equivalence is stabilized by signs of delivery, such as label, class, rarity frame, displayable position and internal commensurability, public continuity can function as a substitute for the preservation of the relevant enjoyment<1>p. 313</1>

[...] public continuity can function as a substitute for the preservation of the relevant enjoyment, so that restoring comes to mean preserving recognizable symptoms of persistence, even if restrictions, effects, modes of access and performance conditions that constituted the acquired position are altered from within<1>p. 313</1>

The legal problem is not the symbolic, but the practical neutralization of the proof of the link between promise and enjoyment, which requires criteria of traceability and substantive control of equivalence.<1>p. 313</1>
<1>Hypercuratorial anticipation</1>

And there is what has not even arrived yet. The platform announces the next event, the skin that will come back, the one that will disappear and the next season. It releases short, cryptic trailers, shows the plan for the year and sets dates. The future stops being only your expectation and becomes a calendar that the company organizes and sells.

The present thus becomes a waiting room. You stay on standby for the next cycle, the next update and the next opportunity. And the waiting becomes part of what you consume, as if the announcement were already a piece of the delivery. The platform sells not just the now but also your staying on, waiting for what comes next.

Hypercuratorial anticipation designates an economic-semiological technique by which the platform produces a consumable future through continuous curation, defining what will come, what will disappear, what will return and what will be raised to the status of “event”.<1>p. 313</1>
The consumer is kept in continuous readiness for “the next cycle”, “the next update”, “the next opportunity”<1>p. 314</1>
The present stops being the place of a stabilized delivery and becomes a governed antechamber<1>p. 314</1>

Thus, the platform does not sell only the “now”, since it also sells permanence oriented to the “yet to come”, converting expectation into an asset and transforming waiting into a material component of enjoyment.<1>p. 314</1>

Instead of the future appearing as a simple expectation of the consumer, it is produced as an institutional calendar and as a repertoire of signs, with release cuts, schedule forecasts, teasers and updates that become, in practice, part of what sustains permanence and decision.<1>p. 314</1>
So is desiring a skin a mistake?

None of this means that desiring a skin is a mistake, or that every ad, every draw or every pretty shop window is illegal. Selling, persuading and running a game are not abuses in themselves. What matters here is something else. Because the skin's value is made of signs, and because the platform controls those signs, it can tinker with the value of what you bought without touching the item. That is what needs to be visible and comparable, and something you can demand.
This is not about investigating the subjective psychological intention of business agents, nor about moralizing every form of monetization, persuasion or private governance<1>p. 732</1>
What matters for the argument of the simulacrum is not the moralization of gacha<1>p. 299</1>
The legal contribution of the simulacrum, therefore, is not to treat consumption as illusion, but to make nameable the practical displacement of the criterion of performance.<1>p. 313</1>
<1>What was promised has to be delivered</1><2>What was promised has to be delivered</2>
When does advertising become part of the offer?

When the purchase comes after careful preparation. It may be a countdown, a promise of exclusivity, a warning that it will run out, a status signal or the suggestion that one item is worth as much as another. In these cases, advertising stops being just advertising and becomes part of the offer itself.
What does the announcement oblige the platform to deliver?

It must make what was announced match what is delivered. The promise, the announced value and the costs that were not shown have to match the experience you receive, including after the platform changes the game.
How do you compare the promise with what was delivered?
What the sales environment was like, which ads were running, what was featured, how the item was presented and what happened afterwards, compared with what was promised.
What do you ask for when the promise is not kept?

That the offer be corrected and fulfilled, that what you lost be restored and that the misleading communication stop. In some cases, you can ask for sales strategies incompatible with what is really delivered to be struck down. Depending on the case, the law may treat this as misleading or abusive advertising, or as an offer that binds whoever made it.
Is pushy advertising a problem in itself?
What counts is not whether the advertising is lively or pushy. It is the relationship between what was presented before and what you were able to use afterwards.

Whenever enjoyment is preceded by curated cycles of anticipation, promise, suggested scarcity, symbolic distinction or insinuated equivalences, advertising will materially be part of the offer.<1>p. 744-745</1>
The corresponding supply duty is to ensure correspondence between promise, announced value, hidden costs and the experience actually made available under managed mutability.<1>p. 745</1>

The minimum required proof involves reconstruction of the promotional environment, of the communication pieces, of the symbolic saliences, of the context of presentation of the object and of the relationship between prior promise and later enjoyment.<1>p. 745</1>
The legal qualification may fall under misleading or abusive advertising, binding offer, abusive practice through managed ambiguity<1>p. 745</1>

The possible institutional consequence covers correction of the offer, functional restoration, injunctive relief over the communication and, depending on the case, invalidation of promotional strategies incompatible with the real experience delivered.<1>p. 745</1>
