What if the loss is part of the plan?
The floor plan of a store in which every aisle, by different routes, ends at the same checkout. The hidden lines of the design appear in orange.
A bad change may be just a mistake, and mistakes happen. But the picture changes when you look at everything together, instead of one thing at a time.

Staged rarity, manufactured haste, the promise of progress, the fear of losing what you have built up and the small downgrades that never stop seem trivial when seen one by one. Together, they squeeze the time you have to think, raise the cost of leaving, make it harder to go back and leave you more and more dependent on the very place that governs what you use.
That is why exploitation almost never appears in a scandalous clause or in an advertisement that lies on its own. It appears as an operating program, what the service does every day.

What occurs, more often, is the combination of staged scarcity, manufactured urgency, promise of progression, diffuse threat of loss, gradual downgrades of utility and symbolic anchoring of permanence<1>p. 670</1>
In IOC ecosystems, exploitation rarely presents itself in the clean form of a scandalous clause or of an advertisement that lies in isolation. It tends to emerge as an operating program<1>p. 670</1>

It tends to emerge as an operating program, that is, as an articulation of multiple mechanisms that compress reflection time, reorganize expectation, increase exit cost, hinder reversal and make enjoyment progressively dependent on the very environment that governs it<1>p. 670</1>
<1>Abusive teleology</1>

Teleology means purpose. It becomes abusive when the way the service is supplied comes to aim, in practice, at exploiting the fragility of the people who use it. Or at hiding what is lost, or at turning each change into a way of locking you in and charging you.

The most important point here is that nobody has to guess at intentions. The question is not what was going on in anyone's head at the company, and not every way of selling, persuading or running a game stands condemned. What gets examined is where the design points, judged by the pattern that repeats, the coherence among the pieces and the effect it produces again and again.

Abusive teleology thus describes a situation in which the practical purpose of the supply arrangement departs from legally tolerable limits and comes to orient the environment toward structural exploitation of vulnerability, toward relevant obscuring of enjoyment or toward recurrent conversion of mutability into a technology of capture.<1>p. 732</1>

This is not about investigating the subjective psychological intention of business agents, nor about moralizing every form of monetization, persuasion or private governance. The focus is on the functional purpose objectively inscribed in the arrangement, as revealed by its replicability, its internal coherence and its repeated impact on the consumer's experience.<1>p. 732</1>
The category does not depend on imputing subjective psychological intention or on locating a single act as a sufficient cause<1>p. 448</1>
Does the abusive purpose pass the five questions?
So that it does not become a catch-all label, the abusive purpose has to pass a five-question test, and every answer must be yes.

Is the purpose written into the design itself? It has to show up in screen choices, in the terms of use, in the access rules and in the way penalties are applied, and not be just a side effect that happened once.
Does it repeat as a pattern? An isolated episode, a mistake or an exception is not enough.

Does it take advantage of weaknesses that are built into the arrangement? For example, how hard it is to understand what is going on, the dependence of someone who has already invested a lot, the cost of switching games and the loss of the reputation, friends and history built there.

Does it come with a lack of clarity and little room to contest? It is not enough for the system to be complex. The way it works has to make it hard to understand and question the decisions that matter.
And does it seriously and lastingly affect what you bought, even without taking everything away at once? A mere fluctuation in the service does not count.
For this qualification to remain controllable and not turn into an elastic label, it must take the form of a test composed of cumulative elements<1>p. 448</1>

The first requirement is inscribed teleology. It must be possible to reconstruct that the exploitative purpose is not merely an occasional side effect, but appears embedded in design choices, terms of use, authorization mechanisms and enforcement strategies that structure the environment of enjoyment.<1>p. 448</1>
The second requirement is reproduction as a pattern. The deviation cannot be an isolated episode, a contingent error or an operational exception.<1>p. 448</1>

The exploitative purpose must bear on asymmetries of intelligibility and agency that are part of the very arrangement of governed consumption, such as semiotic vulnerability, dependence through captivity, migration costs and loss of investments accumulated in reputation, networks or history.<1>p. 449</1>

The fourth requirement is opacity combined with low contestability. It is not enough for the system to be complex or to operate with metrics. The mode of operation must structurally hinder the understanding and challenging of the relevant decisions<1>p. 455</1>
Abusive teleology must produce a substantial and persistent impact on the practical conditions of use and value of the acquired object, even if there is no total interruption.<1>p. 455</1>
The requirement prevents the category from being triggered by any fluctuation in the service<1>p. 455</1>
Is an aggressive business already pursuing an abusive purpose?

This is not a catch-all label. Charging, persuading and governing a game are not abuses in themselves. Nor is it enough for a business to be merely aggressive, for a design to be debatable or for an arrangement to be simply efficient for the company.

And there are legitimate purposes that the platform can and should pursue, such as security, stability and game balance. The abusive purpose appears only when it can be shown, with reasons, that the design is aimed mainly at exploiting your weakness and capturing value disproportionately, and not at those ends.
Abusive teleology cannot function as a moral wild card.<1>p. 456</1>
[...] abusive teleology is not to be confused with a merely harsh business choice, with debatable design or with architecture that is simply efficient for the supplier.<1>p. 666</1>

It must depend on the rational demonstration that the architecture is oriented, predominantly, toward the exploitation of vulnerability and the disproportionate capture of value, with persistent opacity and asymmetry, and not toward legitimate purposes of the service, such as security, stability and the balance of the ecosystem.<1>p. 456</1>
This formulation is no license for judicial impressionism or for abstract moralizing about the digital environment.<1>p. 666</1>
<1>Unlawful act of architecture</1>
We are used to looking for abuse in a contract clause, in a sentence you can underline. But sometimes no clause on its own is the problem.

The problem is the pattern that repeats. Options that come pre-checked, friction whenever you try to do what you want, manufactured urgency and a cancellation path that seems designed to make you give up. And also equivalences that shift whenever it suits the company, penalties that are hard to understand and proof that is impossible to gather. When these pieces work together as a method, in a stable way, the problem is no longer only in the text. It is in the design.

That is why it is said that, in these cases, design is also conduct. The way the service was built is treated as something the company does, and answers for, and not as a neutral setting where things simply happen.

The unlawful act does not arise, therefore, from a singular episode that can be treated as an accident. It emerges when defaults, frictions, manufactured urgencies, hostile cancellation routes, elastic equivalences, sanction regimes or proof arrangements work together as a method of exploitation.<1>p. 666</1>

When this governance repeatedly organizes informational noise, decisional friction, evidentiary opacity, non-auditable mutation and insufficient restoration, the unlawful act is no longer only in the statement. It is in the architecture.<1>p. 664</1>
The core of the parameter lies in treating architecture as conduct.<1>p. 732</1>
What is called into question is not design as style, visual language or interface aesthetics<1>p. 664</1>
Is everything innovation, or is everything in the contract?

This avoids two common mistakes. The first is accepting that everything is innovation, as if the mere fact that the platform changes all the time left it free to downgrade anything. The second is hunting for loose clauses in the contract, as if the service could only be controlled in pieces of text and never in the way it works.

What is needed, in the end, are familiar criteria. Information you can really understand, respect for trust, equivalence of what was bought, changes that leave a trace, a real possibility of undoing what was done and at least some chance to contest. When the design starts working against these criteria, the service itself becomes an instrument of exploitation.

The first would be to dissolve the problem in the vague language of “innovation” or of the platform's “dynamic nature”, as if the continuous reorganization of the environment were enough to immunize any relevant downgrading of enjoyment. The second would be to reduce the legal response to the atomized hunt for isolated clauses, as if supply could only be controlled in its textual fragments and never in its operational logic.<1>p. 664</1>

And these criteria have already been prepared over the preceding course of the argument: material intelligibility of information, protection of trust, functional value equivalence, open auditability, real possibility of reversal and minimum conditions of contestation.<1>p. 664</1>

Abusive teleology arises precisely when the design of supply stops respecting these parameters and comes to operate against them, converting the very structure of the service into an instrument of exploitation.<1>p. 664</1>
<1>Law</1>Dark patterns

Some screen traps already have a name known worldwide, dark patterns. Examples include the box that comes pre-checked so you sign up for an extra service, the cancel button hidden in light gray and the warning that only a few units are left when that is not true.

What matters in these cases is not an isolated sentence but the way choices are presented and steered. And Brazilian consumer protection law already allows many cases of deceptive design to be punished. Design thus stops being treated as neutral aesthetics and goes back to being what it is, a commercial practice with an economic goal, which the law can characterize.

[...] the asymmetry of intelligibility and agency can be produced and exploited by the interaction architecture itself, making the design of options and avenues of reaction legally relevant [...] This point becomes clearer when interface patterns are described as a sanctionable commercial practice, since abusiveness stops depending on an isolated textual statement and comes to include the way choices are presented and induced<1>p. 405</1>

several of these provisions are related to dark patterns, which allows us to conclude that under the Brazilian legal framework it is possible to sanction several cases of deceptive design<1>p. 405</1>

When it is recognized that it is possible to sanction cases of deceptive design and the provisions of art. 39 of the CDC<1><2>1</2></1> are linked to dark patterns, design is put back in its correct place, as an economically oriented and legally qualifiable commercial practice, and not as aesthetic neutrality<3>p. 432</3>
It emerges when defaults, frictions, manufactured urgencies, hostile cancellation routes<1>p. 666</1>
<1>Misleading advertising by architecture</1><2><3>Misleading advertising by architecture</3></2>
An advertisement does not need to lie to deceive. It can tell the truth in pieces and lie as a whole, just by the way it organizes what you see first and what is left for later.

It works like this. The good side of the purchase goes to the center of the screen, big and colorful. The cost, the chance that things will change and the limits go to the footer, to a link that only appears later or to a layer nobody opens when deciding. Each piece of information is there, but taken together they lead you to the wrong understanding, and it is that whole that the law can examine.

In simpler terms, communication does not need to lie to deceive. It is enough that it manages the interpretive framing in a sufficiently asymmetric way. Advertising can tell the truth in pieces and still lie as a whole.<1>p. 626</1>

This is the core of misleading advertising by semiotic architecture. The architecture of the advertisement becomes legally relevant when the supplier structures the consumer's understanding so as to reinforce the positive side of the experience and push the onerous, mutable or limited side out of focus<1>p. 626</1>

It can be produced by the way the essential is ranked, by selective emphasis on advantages and by the displacement of relevant conditions to disclaimers, low-visibility layers, later links or discursive zones that do not usefully form part of the decisional moment<1>p. 626</1>
<1>Biographical continuity</1><2><3>Biographical continuity</3></2>
When an account is deleted, you do not lose just one item. You lose the whole position, the history, the inventory, the trajectory and your place in that world.

Your story there was made of repeated choices, performance, time, purchases, cooperation with other players and signs of belonging built up over years. It was built under the platform's rules, but it is still yours, because it is the result of what you did. That is why protection can include the continuity of this biography, and not only a refund for a purchase that went wrong.

The clause is valuable because it lays the problem bare: what is lost is not only an isolated item, but the global position of enjoyment, the history, the inventory, the trajectory and the practical continuity of insertion in the ecosystem<1>p. 540-541</1>

It is a biographical result produced by repeated choices, performance, investment of time, acquisition, cooperation, accumulation of signs of belonging and permanence in the ecosystem. Even though this construction takes place under the mediation of the Lex Plataformae, it remains attributable to the consumer as an expression of biographical continuity within the supply regime.<1>p. 537</1>

Thus, what is asserted is only that the consumer's integrity may include the preservation of minimum conditions of biographical continuity and stability of symbolic insertion, and not only the refund of a frustrated purchase<1>p. 537</1>

In serious cases, losing the account, the history or the trajectory can harm your personality rights and give rise to moral damages, that is, compensation for harm that is not financial. This happens when the loss affects, in a way that can be shown, your story, your belonging or the reputation and memory you built in there.

Not every annoyance reaches this point, and so you have to show what was affected. But when everything changes and you no longer feel the same, that is not drama or a passing irritation. It is the foreseeable consequence of a regime in which the value of what you use and your place in the game depend on someone else's management.

In qualified cases, the loss of account, history or trajectory may constitute moral damages for injury to personality, especially when it objectively affects biographical continuity, institutionalized belonging in the ecosystem or relevant anchors of reputation and memory, and not mere subjective displeasure.<1>p. 541</1>

When everything changes and the consumer does not feel the same, this is not subjective drama or mere displeasure. It is the foreseeable consequence of a regime in which use value, symbolic value and continuity of enjoyment are subject to the governance of third parties.<1>p. 21</1>

And consumer law already has doors for this. When the design takes usefulness away from what you bought, the door is the rule on quality defects. When it pushes your choice with invented scarcity, manufactured haste and hurdles on one side only, the door is the rule on abusive practices. And when all this becomes a rule written into the terms, the door is the rule on abusive clauses.
There is no need to invent a new law for platforms. What changes is what these doors can see, which is no longer just the episode but the pattern that produces the loss.

The first axis of framing falls on the quality defect, whenever the operating program of the service produces a relevant loss of adequacy, continuity or functional equivalence of enjoyment.<1>p. 674</1>
The second axis of framing falls on abusive practices, and it is here that abusive teleology appears most strongly as a repeated method of exploitation.<1>p. 676</1>
When artificial scarcity, manufactured urgency, cycles of promise, fabrication of risk, asymmetric frictions and hindered reversibility operate in a predictable and repeated way<1>p. 676</1>
The third axis is that of abusive clauses, whenever the exploitative program gains contractual institutionalization in predisposed terms, policies and acceptances.<1>p. 677</1>
It does not require leaving the CDC or inventing a parallel law of platforms.<1>p. 679</1>
This is how legal control stops aiming only at the episode and comes to reach the governance pattern that produces, reinforces or normalizes the injury.<1>p. 679</1>
<1>When loss is the rule, the problem is the design</1><2>When loss is the rule, the problem is the design</2>
When does loss become part of the game's routine?

When several small things work together to take advantage of your weaknesses or to make your experience worse as a matter of routine. They are small frictions that wear you down, losses everyone already treats as normal and manufactured urgency. They are also artificial scarcity, a lack of clarity that works in the company's favor and equivalences that shift whenever it suits the company.

You do not need to prove that someone wanted to harm you. What matters is the purpose that shows in the very functioning of the environment. It can be seen in the pattern that repeats, the coherence among the pieces and the effect produced again and again.
What must the game's design not aim at?
It must not build the experience around an exploitative purpose that goes against good faith, transparency and balance, or that disregards what you legitimately acquired.
How do you show that the problem forms a pattern?

By showing the pattern, the fact that it repeats and the way the pieces of the environment combine. And the relevant impact this has on your freedom of choice in practice, on your understanding or on the utility of what you use.
Can you ask for more than fixing one case?

Yes, more than fixing one episode. You can ask for the game's paths to be redone, for transparency to increase and for the design to be corrected. When this design produces a pattern of injury that repeats, the response can also reach the structure that reproduces it.
Is every way of selling and persuading abusive?
Not every way of selling, persuading or running the game is abusive. What is controlled is a program that can be recognized in the functioning of the environment, and not someone's hidden will.

Whenever microfrictions, normalized losses, manufactured urgencies, artificial scarcities, strategic opacity, elastic equivalences and other mechanisms operate in a coordinated way to extract value from vulnerability or degrade enjoyment as a routine of the environment, there will be a case of abusive teleology.<1>p. 746</1>

The corresponding supply duty is not to structure the experience on the basis of an exploitative purpose incompatible with good faith, transparency, balance and protection of the enjoyment legitimately incorporated into the bond.<1>p. 746</1>

The minimum required proof consists of demonstrating the pattern, its replicability, the coordination between mechanisms of the ecosystem and the relevant impact produced on practical autonomy, intelligibility or utility of the experience.<1>p. 746-747</1>

The institutional consequence goes beyond redress of isolated episodes and may include reconfiguration of flows, reinforced duties of transparency, design correction and structural or collective measures.<1>p. 747</1>
What is controlled is not an inner will, but a recognizable program<1>p. 732</1>
If the law needs to see all this, does it already have the means?

Who profits from your click?
A castle made of server blocks on top of clouds. Down below, people play, and each of their gestures rises like a brick that makes the castle bigger.

The company that set up the store is the same one that controls the game, the rules, the updates and what other players see. The skin stays in your account, and on paper it is yours, but it is the platform that decides how useful it is, how much it shines and how long it stays worth anything.

This changes what it costs to be there. Staying does not cost only the next payment, because it also costs attention, adaptation, loss of equivalence when things change and a dependence that never ends. And the company does not profit only at the moment of purchase. It profits by managing the place every day, with invented rarity, update cycles and changes of meaning that push you into another round of spending.
The platform operates as an infrastructure landlord: it controls the environment, the rules, the updates and the visibility of what acquires value there.<1>p. 146</1>

“Cloud capital” appears as dominion over access, reputation and permanence, so that the consumer, although preserving formal ownership over items linked to the account, remains subject to the unilateral power to modulate utility, prestige and conditions of enjoyment. The cost is expressed not only in a new payment, but also in attention, adaptation, loss of equivalence and continuous dependence on the administered territory.<1>p. 146</1>

Rent is extracted not only at the act of purchase, but in the continuous management of the digital territory, where artificial scarcity, update cycles and reconfiguration of signs reorganize desires and push the subject into new rounds of spending and recomposition of status.<1>p. 146</1>
<1>Political economy</1>Technofeudalism

In feudal times there were lords, who owned the land, and serfs, who lived and worked on it under the lord's rules. Some say that today the land has become the cloud. The owners of the servers, the platforms and the algorithms play the part of the new lords, and those who use these places live under their rules.

You do not stop consuming because of this. The point is that, each time you take part, you help grow the same power that governs you. That is why people speak of cloud serfs. And, in the case of the game, the fief is not even a figure of speech, because it has a name and an address, which is your account.

The author argues that the capitalist system would be on the way to being replaced by what he calls “technofeudalism”, in which capital stops presenting itself primarily as material property and comes to concentrate “in the cloud”, that is, in digital assets, online platforms and algorithms.<1>p. 142</1>
The author reintroduces a feudal grammar to describe the present, in which the owners of cloud capital appear as new feudal lords, while the rest return to the condition of serfs.<1>p. 151</1>

Hence the force of the feudal image: consumers and users become “cloud serfs” not because they stop consuming, but because their participation comes to reproduce the very capital that governs them.<1>p. 146</1>
The fief is not a metaphor for the digital environment. It is an account.<1>p. 153</1>
Why is the skin not like a refrigerator?

An ordinary purchase is different. When you buy a refrigerator, it goes to your home and from then on exists out of the seller's reach, at least for as long as a refrigerator can be expected to last. The store profits once and that is it.

The skin is different, because it only works inside a place you do not control. It goes through updates, balance adjustments, the end of events, catalog changes, changes in the game's currency and new policies. That is why the platform does not profit only from delivering the skin. It also profits by controlling access and time, that is, by charging for passage, for staying and for the predictability of a place that it governs itself.

In the industrial economy, the consumer pays to acquire a good whose existence, once purchased, tends to stabilize out of the supplier's reach, at least within reasonable expectations of durability and of the discipline of defects.<1>p. 210</1>

The consumer does not buy a “thing” and take it with them; they enter an access regime in which the object remains functional only within the infrastructure they do not control, crossed by updates, balancing, closing of events, catalog rotation, reconfigurations of internal currency and policy changes<1>p. 210</1>
The consequence is that the platform stops monetizing only the delivery of a good and comes to monetize control of access and time.<1>p. 209</1>
It does not sell a “thing”, it sells passage, permanence and predictability in an environment it governs itself<1>p. 209</1>
<1>Political economy</1>Toll economy

Some earn less from what they deliver and more because everyone is forced to go through their turnstile. The services may even be useful, but the profit comes mainly from the point of passage that nobody can avoid.

In the game, this toll is not charged just once. The platform charges for entry, charges for the hurry of anyone who wants to get there first, charges for convenience, charges for what sets you apart from others and charges for the return of an item that had gone away. And, above all, it charges for protection against a risk it created itself, such as the fear of missing the next window.
Rentiers earn not so much from the services they provide as from everyone's obligation to pass through their turnstiles.<1>p. 185</1>
Many services are useful, or even necessary, but generate disproportionate profits relative to the contribution<1>p. 185</1>

The platform monetizes access in layers: it charges for entry, charges for acceleration, charges for convenience, charges for symbolic differentiation, charges for return and, above all, charges for mitigating the risk it fabricates itself.<1>p. 210</1>
The toll does not present itself only as an entry price. It reappears as a repeated charge for permanence, organized around time, attention and the predictability of cycles.<1>p. 210</1>
Who decides what the game's currency is worth?

The game's currency, the one you buy with real money and then trade for skins, shows the same power. The terms of use admit that the company may, at times, change what this currency buys, including asking for more coins for the same skin. The same company sets the currency, the catalog and the price, and that is why it can gradually raise prices inside the game without facing the competition of an open market.

The same contract goes a step further and says that the data stored on the company's servers, including the content of your account, has no value at all. The effect is direct. If on paper your collection is worth nothing, inflation inside the game looks natural, and not like a loss you suffered. And, as if that were not enough, the contract tries to limit the company's liability to what you paid in the twelve months before the problem, precisely in a place where value comes from years of accumulation.

The terms admit that, “at times”, the company may alter the purchasing power of the Game Currency, including increasing the number of coins needed to acquire virtual products such as skins, and place this movement under the generic promise of notice and gradualness <1>Riot Games</1><2>(Riot Games, 2024e)</2>.<3>p. 176</3>

By defining the catalog, modulating scarcity, managing windows of opportunity and operating internal currencies, bundles and conversions, the supplier comes to calibrate the general level of prices charged, gradually raising price references and shifting anchors of acceptability without facing the discipline typical of markets with open supply and demand<1>p. 176</1>
The contract expressly denies any value attributed to data residing on servers operated or controlled by Riot, including Game Content and Virtual Content associated with the account.<1>p. 176</1>

If the collection is legally described as having no value, internal inflation and the loss of purchasing power come to be treated as a natural variation of the fief, not as deterioration of an economic position relevant to the consumer<1>p. 176-177</1>
The limitation clause provides that total liability may be limited to the amounts paid by the user in the 12 months prior to the cause arising<1>p. 177</1>

The platform reserves the power to govern value, currency and access within the territory, but tries to downgrade the civil response for losses to a calculation that ignores precisely what makes the fief efficient, which is prolonged accumulation, dependence and exit cost<1>p. 177</1>
How do small losses become a big bill?

A dripping faucet works like this. Each drop seems like nothing, but at the end of the month the bill arrives. Many platforms do not live only on large, visible charges. They also live on small events, small decisions and small losses, spread across millions of people and almost invisible one by one.

Added up, they weigh a lot. But each one stays too small to be worth a fight, and that is where the trick lies. The profit comes from repetition at scale, always below the point at which someone would bother to complain or to punish.

The engine of many digital ecosystems is not only overt charging, but drainage through microevents, microdecisions and microlosses, distributed at scale and diluted to the point of becoming almost invisible, although cumulatively relevant.<1>p. 26</1>

[...] the boundary between lawful and unlawful stops functioning as an effective prohibition and comes to operate as an optimization parameter of the business model itself, in which profit is realized not by a high margin on few units, but by scale and repetition below the punishable threshold<1>p. 26</1>

A dripping faucet. Each drop carries a tiny object, a coin, a small clock, a small heart, and the bucket below is already almost full.
Who decides when a skin becomes rare?

How does something that can be copied for free become rare? A digital skin could be sold to everyone, forever, without running out. If it disappears, comes back only sometimes or becomes a last chance, that is not the nature of the object. It is the company's choice.

The platform creates sales windows, store rotations, rarity tiers, seasonal events, passes, countdowns and limited bundles. Then it turns this arrangement into a story, with words like rare, exclusive, last chance, collectible and special edition. That is how something that was not scarce becomes scarce, by design.

In digital objects, the marginal cost of reproduction tends to fall drastically and, in theory, availability could expand without requiring productive capacity comparable to the factory, logistics and extraction of inputs.<1>p. 209</1>

For this reason, when a persistent regime of unavailability, exclusivity and last chance is observed in these markets, what one faces is not a natural condition of the object, but a deliberate institutional choice, so that scarcity appears not as a fact, but as a project<1>p. 209</1>

The platform creates windows, rotations, tiers, seasonal events, passes, countdowns, limited bundles and conditioned acquisition mechanisms. It then converts this arrangement into narrative, speaking of “rarity”, “exclusive”, “last chance”, “collectible” and “special edition”.<1>p. 209</1>
The non-scarce is made scarce by design<1>p. 209</1>
And when the exclusive skin comes back cheaper?

A skin is sold at a high price because it is exclusive, and exclusivity is part of the price. Months later, the same skin comes back in an alternative store, in a special currency or in an aggressive promotion, for much less. And nobody had told you, clearly, at the time of purchase, that the exclusivity had an expiry date.
